"Well, you see, here's how it happened. Old missus—that's Miss Watson—she's always finding fault with me and treating me pretty badly, but she always said she wouldn't sell me down to Orleans. Lately, though, I'd noticed a slave trader coming around the place a lot, and I started getting nervous. Then one night I crept up to the door quite late. It wasn't completely closed, and I heard old missus telling the widow she was going to sell me down to Orleans. She said she didn't want to, but she could get eight hundred dollars for me, and that was so much money she couldn't resist. The widow tried to make her promise she wouldn't do it, but I didn't stay to hear any more. I got out of there mighty quick, I tell you.

"I hurried down the hill, planning to steal a little boat somewhere along the shore above town. But people were still moving around, so I hid in the old ruined barrel-making shop on the bank, waiting for everybody to leave. Well, I stayed there all night. Somebody was always nearby. Around six in the morning, boats started going past, and by eight or nine, people in every boat were talking about your pap coming to town and saying you'd been killed. Those later boats were full of ladies and gentlemen going over to see the place. Sometimes they'd stop along the shore for a rest before crossing, and their talk told me everything about the killing. I was terribly sorry you'd been killed, Huck, but I'm not anymore.

"I lay under the wood shavings all day. I was hungry, but I wasn't scared. I knew old missus and the widow were leaving for the camp meeting right after breakfast and staying away all day. They know I go off with the cattle around dawn, so they wouldn't expect to see me at the house and wouldn't miss me until after dark. The other servants wouldn't miss me either, because they'd slip away and take a holiday as soon as the old folks were gone.

"When darkness came, I headed up the river road and walked two miles or more, until there weren't any houses. I'd worked out what I was going to do. You see, if I kept trying to escape on foot, the dogs would follow my trail. If I stole a boat to cross the river, they'd notice it was missing. Then they'd know roughly where I'd landed on the other bank and where to start looking for my tracks.

It is only four in the afternoon, but in this winter season the sun has already gone down. No clouds hang in the clear, freezing sky to catch its slanting rays, yet the air itself holds a faint pink glow, reflected in turn upon the snow covering the earth. I live in an isolated cottage on a vast, deserted heath; no sound of living voices reaches me. The empty plain stretches white before my eyes, broken only by a few dark patches where the midday sun has cleared the tops of pointed hillocks. There the snow slipped as it fell and settled less thickly than on level ground. A few birds peck at the solid ice over the pools, for the frost has lasted a long time.

My state of mind is strange. I am alone—utterly alone—in the world. Misfortune has swept across my life and left me withered. I know I am going to die, and I feel happy—joyful. I take my pulse: it is racing. I press my thin hand to my cheek: it burns. A fragile, restless spirit within me is giving off its final sparks. I will never see another winter's snow; I truly believe I will never again feel the life-giving warmth of a summer sun. With this conviction I begin to set down my tragic history. Perhaps a story like mine ought to die with me, but an indefinable feeling urges me forward, and I am too weak in mind and body to resist even the slightest impulse. When life still ran strongly through me, I believed my story possessed a sacred horror that made speaking of it impossible. Now, as death approaches, I profane its mysterious terrors. It resembles the grove of the Eumenides, which only the dying may enter; and Oedipus is approaching death.

What am I writing? I must gather my thoughts. I do not know whether anyone will read these pages besides you, my friend, who will receive them when I die. I will not address them to you alone, because it will comfort me to describe our friendship in ways that would be unnecessary if you were my only reader. I shall therefore tell my story as though writing for strangers. You have often asked why I live alone, why I weep, and above all why I maintain this impenetrable, unkind silence. During life I could not dare explain; in death I reveal the mystery. Others may turn these pages carelessly. To you, Woodville, my kind and loving friend, they will be precious: the treasured record of a brokenhearted girl who, even dying, still feels the warmth of gratitude toward you. Your tears will fall upon the words describing my misfortunes—I know they will—and while I am alive, I thank you for your compassion.

But no; a prospect more dazzling still awaited him. He would turn pirate! That was the answer! Now his future stood clear before him, shining with a magnificence beyond imagining. How his name would travel through the world and set people trembling! How splendidly he would cleave the leaping seas in his swift, long, low, black-hulled vessel, the Spirit of the Storm, its dreadful flag streaming at the fore! And when his fame was at its height, how suddenly he would return to the old village and stride into church, tanned and weather-worn, wearing his black velvet doublet and trunks, his enormous jack-boots, his scarlet sash, a belt crowded with horse-pistols, and his cutlass rusted with crime at his side! With plumes waving on his slouched hat and his black skull-and-crossbones banner spread, he would listen in mounting rapture to the murmurs: "It's Tom Sawyer the Pirate!—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!"

Yes, the matter was decided; his calling was fixed. He would flee home and begin it. He would leave the very next morning, so preparations must start at once. He needed to assemble his resources. Going to a decayed log nearby, he dug beneath one end with his Barlow knife. Before long he hit a piece of wood that gave a hollow sound. He laid his hand upon it and solemnly pronounced the charm:

"Whatever hasn't come here, come! Whatever's here, remain!"

He then scraped off the earth and uncovered a pine shingle. Lifting it, he revealed a neatly made little treasury, lined at the sides and bottom with shingles. Inside rested one marble. Tom was astonished beyond measure. Scratching his head in bewilderment, he exclaimed:

"Well, that beats everything!"

He flung the marble aside in irritation and stood pondering. A superstition which he and all his companions had considered unfailing had, in fact, let him down. Bury a marble with the proper incantations, leave it untouched for a fortnight, then open its hiding place with the charm he had just spoken, and all the marbles you had ever lost would have assembled there meanwhile, however far apart they had scattered. Yet this time the thing had plainly, indisputably failed. The foundations of Tom's entire faith were shaken. He had often heard of its success, never before of its failure. He did not remember that he himself had attempted it several times already, only to lose the hiding places afterward. He puzzled over this for a while, finally concluding that a witch must have meddled and spoiled the spell.
